transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-06 14:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Natarajan (Redwood SE), Sara Gomez (MedConnect Head of Data), Dr. Ben Lewis (MedConnect ML Engineer), Mark Chu (CTO), Tina Park (Product)

[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, we wanted to run through the POC scoping and specifically the quality evaluation plan for the triage assistant - make sure we're aligned on success criteria and benchmarks.

[00:18] Sara Gomez: thanks Alex. high level - we're trying to replace a rules-based routing for incoming patient messages, so accuracy and safety are the big ones. cost matters but not first priority. timeline is tight, ideally pilot in october.

[00:35] Priya Natarajan: great, Priya here. from an SE perspective we'll want golden prompts, regression tests, hallucination checks, and automated scoring so you can measure drift. thinking to run an initial bench of 10k prompts across your typical distribution. is 10k realistic?

[00:52] Dr. Ben Lewis: 10k sounds okay, but we can start with 1k golden prompts for the initial quality pass, and then expand. our traffic is bursty, average daily 5k user messages but peak windows get v spiky.

[01:10] Mark Chu: also curious about latency - our product team wants sub 500ms median for message turnaround. how do hosted vs dedicated influence that?

[01:27] Priya Natarajan: good question. hosted can usually hit ~300-500ms p50 depending on model and prompt length; dedicated gives more predictable throughput and lower variance. for the POC we can run both: a hosted baseline, and a dedicated mini-pool to show differences.

[01:45] Sara Gomez: security side - we need SOC2, SSO, KMS for key management, and audit logs. also data residency in the eu for a subset of patients.

[02:00] Alex Kim: noted - we'll include SOC2 docs and the KMS integration details in the pack I send. Redwood Private/Dedicated supports customer-managed keys and VPC.

[02:12] Tina Park: for success criteria, we propose three buckets: correctness (intent/classification accuracy), safety (no critical hallucinations), and format compliance (structured output matches our schema). we need thresholds for each.

[02:28] Priya Natarajan: suggested thresholds: format compliance >= 92% on golden prompts, critical hallucination rate < 3% on sampled outputs, intent accuracy >= 88% for first pass. these are adjustable after the first run.

[02:44] Dr. Ben Lewis: how are you defining hallucination? we need to differentiate between 'benign hallucination' and 'critical' - e.g., inventing medical advice is critical.

[03:00] Priya Natarajan: agreed - plan is to have a labeled taxonomy: critical (safety/clinical hallucination), moderate (incorrect factual but non-harmful), and format-only issues. scoring will weight critical failures highest. we'll show examples in the golden prompt doc.

[03:18] Alex Kim: on regression tests - we recommend saving golden prompts and expected outputs, and running nightly automated checks that compute rouge/bertscore plus custom format checks and hallucination detectors. for clinical, we can add rule-based checks for clinical contraindications.

[03:36] Sara Gomez: will Redwood support custom checkers? we have a small rules engine we could share.

[03:43] Priya Natarajan: yes, we can plug in your rule engine as a post-processing step in the eval harness. that will also help run format validations and quick heuristics for hallucination detection.

[03:56] Mark Chu: what's the scoring approach exactly? aggregate score? weighted metrics?

[04:03] Priya Natarajan: we propose a composite score: 40% accuracy (intent/classification), 35% safety (inverse of critical hallucination rate), 15% format compliance, 10% latency/cost penalty. each metric is normalized; we provide the raw numbers too so you can decide weightings.

[04:22] Dr. Ben Lewis: examples please - for safety, if out of 1000 samples 10 critical hallucinations, that is 1% critical => safety metric would map to 99% for that component?

[04:33] Priya Natarajan: yes, essentially safety_score = 100 - critical_hallucination_percent; then composite = weighted sum. we'll include thresholds and a pass/fail gating rule for critical hallucinations (e.g., any >5 critical in 1k fails).

[04:50] Sara Gomez: for golden prompts - we will provide typical triage messages and also edge cases (ambiguous patient statements, multi-intent). how many golden prompts do you need?

[05:00] Priya Natarajan: start with 200 golden prompts covering high-frequency intents + 50 edge cases; that plus 1k de-identified historical messages should give a good initial view. we'll then expand to 10k for throughput/cost benchmarks.

[05:16] Alex Kim: regarding benchmarks - we'll run two benchmark suites: quality suite (golden prompts + annotated expected outputs) and performance suite (10k across typical length distribution to measure throughput/cost/latency). estimated run time for perf bench ~2 hours for a single model variant depending on hardware.

[05:35] Mark Chu: cost estimates when? we need cost per thousand tokens and estimated monthly spend for production.

[05:42] Alex Kim: after the perf run we can extrapolate monthly costs based on your traffic shape. we'll include both hosted charges and a modeled dedicated estimate with reserved capacity assumptions.

[05:58] Tina Park: regression tests - do you keep a baseline model and test new versions automatically?

[06:06] Priya Natarajan: yes, Redwood Optimize supports model rollouts and regression alerts. for the POC we'll set up a baseline and run diffs on new model checkpoints; if composite score drops by X% we'll flag a regression.

[06:20] Dr. Ben Lewis: what about format checks - our product needs strict JSON with fields; how tolerant is Redwood's validator?

[06:29] Priya Natarajan: we have a schema validator step that checks for required keys, types, and can auto-reject outputs that don't parse. we can also attempt auto-fixes like small punctuation adjustments, but those are controlled options. for the POC we suggest strict validation and report any auto-fixes separately.

[06:46] Sara Gomez: data residency again - for EU patients we need processing in eu region, or at least do not leave eu. can the eval harness run regionally?

[06:56] Alex Kim: yes, we can run benchmark jobs in eu region. for dedicated/private we can ensure all processing and KV caches stay in your VPC. we'll include region configuration in the runbook.

[07:10] Mark Chu: timeline - what's realistic to get initial results?

[07:15] Priya Natarajan: proposed timeline: week 0 (this week) collect golden prompts and sample data; week 1 run quality suite and small perf run; week 2 run full 10k perf and iterate on thresholds and report. so about two weeks to a full POC report.

[07:32] Alex Kim: that's what we've done with other healthcare customers. deliverables: draft eval spreadsheet + golden prompt examples (redwood), perf results + cost model (redwood), and final readout call.

[07:42] Tina Park: are there risks we should call out? like prompt leakage, PII in samples, or model hallucination causing false advice - that'll affect our legal sign-off.

[07:53] Priya Natarajan: risk mitigation: require de-identification before upload, use of private/dedicated environment for any PHI, strict access controls and audit logs. we'll also include guardrails (prompt templates, response classifiers) to reduce hallucination risk.

[08:12] Dr. Ben Lewis: any tooling for human-in-the-loop review during pilot? we want labelers to quickly flag hallucinations and format errors.

[08:20] Alex Kim: yes, we'll provide a lightweight review UI and exportable CSVs for your annotators. annotations feed back into the regression suite.

[08:31] Sara Gomez: what about metrics for multi-turn context? our triage uses short conversations, not single-shot prompts.

[08:38] Priya Natarajan: we'll include multi-turn tests in the golden prompts; evaluate context carryover, slot-filling and KV cache behavior. latency will be measured per-turn and for entire session if needed.

[08:52] Mark Chu: competitor question - how would Redwood compare to just calling OpenAI?

[08:58] Alex Kim: short answer: Redwood gives you deployment flexibility (dedicated/private), observability at token level, cost controls and production-focused tooling like caching and rollouts. calling OpenAI is simpler but less control for enterprise requirements.

[09:12] Tina Park: ok last bit, scoring thresholds - can you share the spreadsheet after the call so we can tweak weights?

[09:19] Alex Kim: yes we'll send the draft spreadsheet by friday (2026-10-08). default weights are the composite I mentioned; you can propose changes.

[09:28] Priya Natarajan: one technical note on hallucination detectors - automatic detectors catch many issues but are not perfect; we'll still sample and do human review for the safety metric.

[09:40] Dr. Ben Lewis: agreed, we want a human review sample for every run, say 2% of outputs or min 200 examples.

[09:49] Sara Gomez: recap?

[09:52] Alex Kim: recap: Redwood to send draft quality eval plan + golden prompt template and security pack by 2026-10-08. MedConnect to provide de-id sample prompts (1k) and 200 golden prompts + edge cases by 2026-10-09. Redwood SE to run initial quality suite week of 2026-10-12 and full perf run by 2026-10-16. review call 2026-10-16. success metrics: format >=92%, critical hallucinations <3%, intent accuracy >=88%, latency p50 <=450ms for hosted baseline, dedicated to show lower variance.

[10:20] Mark Chu: that works. thanks everyone.

[10:23] Alex Kim: thanks all - action items captured, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the spreadsheet.

[10:30] (call ends)

Notes: transcript contains some auto-corrections and speaker attribution may have slight errors. References: shared doc link (redwood.io/medconnect/poc-eval) and security pack (redwood.io/security/medconnect).
